content.title: Mission briefing
content.prompt:
You inherit a tiny account page. It looks polished, but several choices make the main task harder for some users.

Your job is not to make it “more accessible” by guessing. Identify each barrier, make the smallest justified repair, then verify the same user path again.

content.title: Mission requirements
content.prompt:
1. Give the page its correct heading semantics.

2. Make the image understandable for its purpose.

3. Replace the fake action control with a native button.

4. Give the email field a real label.

5. Keep the useful instruction about the email field.

6. Make the error message meaningful in words.

7. Preserve a visible focus indication for keyboard users.

8. Do not rely on color alone for the error state.

takeaways: Independently repair a small page with semantic, labeling, keyboard, focus, image, and color barriers, then explain why each repair matters.

content.title: Step 1 — Repair meaning
content.text: Replace the generic page title with an actual heading element. Choose a level that represents the page title.

content.title: Hint 1
content.text: Ask: “Is this content acting as the page’s main heading?”

content.title: Hint 2
content.text: The page title should be represented by h1.

content.title: Step 2 — Repair the image
content.text: Decide whether the avatar contributes information. If the image identifies the account owner, write short alternative text that identifies the person or purpose. If it is purely decorative, do not add meaningless description.

content.title: Step 3 — Repair the action
content.text: Turn the Save control into a real button. Do not solve the problem with more styling.

content.title: Hint 1
content.text: Use the native element that represents an action.

content.title: Hint 2
content.text: You already used this rule in Lesson 1.4.2.

content.title: Step 4 — Repair the form
content.text: Add a visible label and associate it with the input. Keep the useful instruction next to the field.

content.title: One strong repair
content.text:
```html

Use your work email.

```

content.title: Step 5 — Repair the error
content.text: Rewrite the error so the user knows what happened and what to do next. Make the message meaningful even if the color is removed.

content.title: Clear error copy
content.text:
```html

Enter a valid work email address.

```

content.title: Step 6 — Verify the keyboard path
content.text: Start at the top of the page and press Tab. You should be able to reach the interactive controls, see where focus is, and identify the current field or button without using the mouse.

content.title: Step 7 — Explain your repairs
content.text: Write one sentence for each repair explaining the barrier it removed. Your explanations should use the concepts from this module: semantics, labels, instructions, keyboard access, focus, image purpose, and meaning beyond color.

content.title: Mastery gate
content.text: You have completed the mission when you can repair the page without copying a solution, verify the main task by keyboard, and explain why each repair matters to the person using the interface.

content.title: Forge takeaway & Lesson completion
takeaways: The goal is not to memorize a list of accessibility tricks. The goal is to see the interface as a system of information and actions that must remain usable across different ways of perceiving and operating it.
Senior habit: Accessibility is part of engineering quality. Build the barrier out instead of adding a patch after the fact.
nextSteps: Complete the exercises, explain your reasoning, and verify the interface using the user path named in the lesson.
